doc.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996

title: Drumming from age three, piano study, and teachers
summary: Bellson describes his musical family, wanting to play drums after a parade, teachers Knapp, Spivak and Buddy Baker, and why his father steered him to piano; he notes drummers who also compose.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Actually no, see I come from a musical family. My father played all the instruments and had a music store, and there were eight of us, four girls, four boys, and all of us worked in the music store. And when I was about three and a half years old, my father took me to a parade, and you know for a little person, three and a half years old, and that drum section comes by you and you know that whole sound envelopes your whole body. So I pointed my little finger and I said “I want to play that.” So my dad said I was so definite about it, and he was very liberal-minded as far as wanting to start it at a certain time, it didn’t make any difference as long as you had the interest and you wanted to do it, start, you know? So he started me and eventually I had teachers like Roy Knapp in Chicago and then later on it was Murray Spivak in Los Angeles. But in the meantime, by the time I got to be about thirteen years old, he kind of maneuvered me to the piano. Not to play piano as a solo instrument naturally, he just thought it was time for me to learn theory and harmony and composition. And I was against that. But the minute I started and got into it, then I realized that yeah, I like this, because there’s something inside of me that says © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -2-

compose and arrange, and you can always play drums. So that’s what I did. I kept studying hard with my father and then later on when I got on the road I had Buddy Baker, who just retired from Disney Studios as one of their great composers. I started with him in 1947, and he’s still my teacher. We do things like decipher Ravel’s “Daphnis et Chloé” bar by bar you know. But it’s a never ending process you know. You just keep on learning, and that’s the exciting thing about music.
Well the piano was a good idea then.

Yeah it was. Because my father said, you know, it’s all right to play percussion and play drums, that’s wonderful, but some day, if you’re a band leader, you’ll have respect for your men more if you rehearse the band, don’t have somebody else rehearse it. You get out there in front and say well let’s see that’s a G minor seventh chord and somebody’s playing a B natural instead of a B flat. And so he was right.
Oh — a drummer knows that, yes.

Well a lot of the young drummers, well some of the older guys like Tiny Kahn was a great orchestrator, great arranger. And today, Billy Cobham, Steve Gadd, Tony Williams, a lot of these guys are composing and writing, and Harvey Mason, drummers like that you know, not only great percussion players but they’re very sensitive as to what the music is all about.
